items.prompt: Put the layers of the Earth in order, from the outside to the centre.
hints: The Earth is made of layers, a bit like a boiled egg.
The thin outer layer is the one we live on.
Start with the thin rocky layer under your feet.
items.explanation: From the outside in, the Earth has a thin crust, a thick mantle, a liquid outer core and a solid inner core.

items.prompt: Match each layer of the Earth to its description.
pairs: thin outer layer of solid rock
thick layer of hot rock that flows very slowly
solid ball of iron and nickel at the centre
hints: Two layers are made of rock and two are made of metal.
Only one layer is liquid.
Start with the crust. It is the layer we live on.
items.explanation: The crust is thin solid rock, and the mantle is hot rock that flows very slowly. The outer core is liquid iron and nickel, and the inner core is a solid ball of iron and nickel.

items.prompt: Why does Indonesia have so many volcanoes and earthquakes?

options.text: It is close to the equator.
options.why: Many places on the equator have no volcanoes. The edges of plates are what matter.

options.text: It lies where several tectonic plates meet and push against each other.
It has many islands surrounded by sea.
options.why: Many island countries have few volcanoes. Indonesia's volcanoes come from moving plates.

options.text: It has a very hot climate.
options.why: Hot weather does not make volcanoes. Heat from deep inside the Earth does.

hints: The Earth's crust is broken into huge pieces called tectonic plates.
Volcanoes and earthquakes are most common where plates meet.
Think about where Indonesia sits on a map of the plates.
items.explanation: Indonesia lies where several tectonic plates meet, including the Indo-Australian, Eurasian and Pacific plates. Their movement causes earthquakes and lets magma rise to form volcanoes.

items.prompt: Molten rock that has erupted onto the Earth's surface is called ___.
hints: Melted rock has two names, depending on where it is.
While it is still underground, molten rock is called magma.
The word has four letters and rhymes with Java.
items.explanation: Lava is molten rock that has erupted onto the Earth's surface. Before it erupts, while it is still underground, it is called magma.

items.prompt: Tectonic plates move at about the same speed as your fingernails grow. About how far do they move in a year?

options.text: a few metres
options.why: That would be far faster than fingernails grow.

options.text: a few kilometres
options.why: That would be extremely fast. Plates move very slowly.

options.text: no distance, because plates never move
options.why: Plates do move, slowly but all the time.

options.text: a few centimetres

hints: Think about how much your fingernails grow in a month.
Fingernails grow a few millimetres each month.
Multiply a few millimetres by 12 months, then change the answer into centimetres.
items.explanation: Fingernails grow about 3 to 4 mm a month, which is a few centimetres a year. Plates move at about the same rate, and over millions of years that adds up to thousands of kilometres.

items.prompt: Choose all the safe things to do indoors during an earthquake.

options.text: drop down to the floor
take cover under a strong table
hold on until the shaking stops
run outside while the ground is shaking
options.why: Falling glass and bricks make it dangerous to run outside during shaking.

options.text: stand next to a window
options.why: Windows can break and cut you.

options.text: use the lift to get out quickly
options.why: Lifts can stop working. Use the stairs once the shaking has stopped.

hints: During shaking, the biggest danger is things falling on you.
Find something strong to protect your head and body.
Cross out any action that puts you near glass or keeps you moving while the ground shakes.
items.explanation: Dropping down, taking cover and holding on protects you from falling objects. Running outside, standing by windows or using a lift during shaking can put you in more danger.

items.prompt: A strong earthquake shakes the sea floor. Why should people on the coast move to high ground, even if the sea looks calm?

options.text: The beach sand may turn into lava.
options.why: Sand does not turn into lava. The danger is a giant wave.

options.text: A huge wave called a tsunami may arrive within minutes.
Earthquakes always bring heavy rain.
options.why: Earthquakes do not cause rain. The danger comes from the sea.

options.text: High ground is warmer after an earthquake.
options.why: Temperature is not the reason. High ground is safe from a tsunami.

hints: An undersea earthquake can suddenly push a huge amount of water upwards.
That pushed water spreads out as giant waves.
Ask why high ground would be safer than the beach.
items.explanation: An undersea earthquake can push up a huge amount of water, which travels as a tsunami. It can reach the coast within minutes, so people should move to high ground quickly.

items.prompt: In 1912, Alfred Wegener noticed that the coasts of South America and Africa fit together like jigsaw pieces. Fossils of the same small lake reptile were found on both. What did he suggest?

options.text: The continents were once joined and have slowly drifted apart.
The reptile swam across the ocean.
options.why: This small reptile lived in lakes and could not cross a wide ocean.

options.text: People carried the fossils from one continent to the other.
options.why: The fossils were in rocks millions of years old, long before there were people.

options.text: The oceans were once dry land everywhere.
options.why: The matching coastlines and fossils point to moving continents.

hints: Picture a world map and slide South America towards Africa.
A small lake reptile could not have crossed a whole ocean.
Ask how the same reptile could live in two places that are now far apart.
items.explanation: Wegener suggested that the continents were once joined together and have slowly drifted apart. Today we know that moving tectonic plates carry the continents.

items.prompt: The inner core is even hotter than the outer core, but it is solid. Why?

options.text: The inner core is made of ice.
options.why: The inner core is made of iron and nickel at over 5,000 °C.

options.text: The inner core is cold.
options.why: The inner core is the hottest part of the Earth.

options.text: The huge pressure at the centre squeezes it into a solid.
The Sun's gravity keeps it solid.
options.why: The Sun's gravity does not make the core solid. Pressure from the layers above does.

hints: The inner core has the weight of the whole Earth pressing down on it.
Very high pressure can stop a material from melting.
Compare the pressure at the centre with the pressure in the outer core.
items.explanation: The weight of all the layers above creates enormous pressure at the centre. This pressure squeezes the hot iron and nickel so hard that they stay solid.

items.prompt: In 1815, Mount Tambora in Indonesia erupted and threw ash and gases high into the sky. The next year was unusually cold in Europe and North America. Why?

options.text: The volcano cooled the Sun.
options.why: A volcano cannot change the Sun. Something blocked some of its light.

options.text: Lava flowed all the way to Europe.
options.why: Lava from Tambora stayed on the island of Sumbawa.

options.text: The eruption moved the Earth further from the Sun.
options.why: An eruption cannot change the Earth's orbit.

options.text: Tiny particles high in the air blocked some sunlight from reaching the ground.

hints: The eruption sent tiny particles very high into the atmosphere.
Winds high up can carry these particles around the whole world.
Ask what these particles would do to sunlight on its way to the ground.
items.explanation: Tambora threw tiny particles and gases high into the atmosphere, where winds spread them around the world. They reflected some sunlight back into space, so 1816 was unusually cold in many places.

items.prompt: Label the layers of the Earth in this cross-section.

figure.alt: A circle cut open to show four layers. A thin outer ring, then a thick layer, then a thinner layer, and a small solid circle at the centre.

hints: Tap a label, then tap its number.
The crust is the thin layer at the outside.
The inner core is the small ball at the very centre.
items.explanation: From the outside: the thin crust, the thick mantle, the liquid outer core and the solid inner core.

items.prompt: Tap the place inside the volcano where the magma collects before an eruption.

figure.alt: A cross-section of a cone-shaped volcano on the ground. A dark dip is at the top, a thin channel runs down the middle, and a large oval pocket lies underground at the bottom.

hints: Magma is molten rock under the ground.
It collects before it rises.
Find the large space below the surface.
items.explanation: Magma collects in the magma chamber deep under the volcano. It rises up the vent and erupts from the crater.

items.caption: Plates moving at 2 cm a year
items.prompt: A tectonic plate moves about 2 cm every year. Complete the table.
head: Time (years)
Movement (cm)
hints: The plate moves the same amount every year.
Multiply the number of years by the yearly movement.
For 50 years, work out 50 × 2.
items.explanation: Movement is years × 2 cm. So 50 years gives 100 cm and 100 years gives 200 cm.

items.prompt: A plate moves 3 cm each year. How far does it move in one million years? Give your answer in kilometres.
hints: First find the distance in centimetres.
There are 100 cm in a metre and 1000 m in a kilometre.
3 cm × 1 000 000 = 3 000 000 cm. Now change it to kilometres.

items.prompt: Seismic waves from an earthquake travel at 6 km/s. A town is 120 km from the epicentre. How many seconds do the waves take to reach it?
hints: Time = distance ÷ speed.
Check that the units match: km and km/s.
Divide 120 by 6.
items.explanation: Time = 120 km ÷ 6 km/s = 20 s.

items.prompt: A seismograph station 270 km from an earthquake records the waves arriving after 45 seconds. What is the speed of the waves in kilometres per second?
hints: Speed tells you how far something moves each second.
Use speed = distance ÷ time.
Divide 270 by 45.
items.explanation: Speed = 270 km ÷ 45 s = 6 km/s.

items.prompt: What instrument records the shaking of the ground during an earthquake?

options.text: A thermometer
options.why: A thermometer measures temperature.

options.text: A barometer
options.why: A barometer measures air pressure.

options.text: A seismograph
A newtonmeter
options.why: A newtonmeter measures forces, not ground shaking.

hints: The word seismic is about earthquakes.
The instrument draws a wiggly line when the ground moves.
Choose the tool made for the ground, not the air or temperature.
items.explanation: A seismograph records the vibrations of the ground. Scientists use it to find out how strong an earthquake was.

items.prompt: Most of the world's volcanoes and earthquakes happen in a ring around the Pacific Ocean. Why?

options.text: Plates meet and move against each other there.
The Pacific Ocean is the deepest ocean, so it is hottest.
options.why: Depth does not explain the ring. Plate boundaries do.

options.text: The Moon's pull is strongest over the Pacific.
options.why: The Moon does not cause earthquakes.

options.text: Volcanoes grow where it rains the most.
options.why: Rain does not make volcanoes.

hints: Think about the tectonic plates.
Which places have the most plate movement?
Plate edges are where plates collide, pull apart or slide.
items.explanation: The ring follows the edges of several tectonic plates. Where plates push, pull apart or slide, earthquakes and volcanoes are common.

items.prompt: Choose all the layers that are inside the Earth.

options.text: crust
mantle
atmosphere
outer core
inner core

hints: The atmosphere is not inside.
The Earth has four layers from the surface to the centre.
Pick the four layers of rock and metal.
items.explanation: The Earth has four layers: crust, mantle, outer core and inner core. The atmosphere is the air around it.

items.prompt: Sort each hazard by what mainly causes it.
hints: Some hazards can come from both.
A tsunami starts when the sea floor moves.
Lava and ash come from the volcano.
items.explanation: Shaking and cracks mainly come from earthquakes. Lava and ash come from volcanoes. Tsunamis and landslides can follow either.

items.prompt: Put the steps that make a tsunami in order.
items: An earthquake moves the sea floor
A huge amount of water is pushed up
Waves spread out across the ocean
The waves slow down and rise near the coast
hints: Start with the cause.
Waves travel before they reach land.
The last step is what the people on the coast see.
items.explanation: A moving sea floor pushes up water, which makes waves. The waves rise near the coast and flood the land.

items.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: molten rock that has reached the surface
the point on the surface above where an earthquake starts
a huge slab of the Earth's crust
hints: The difference between magma and lava is where the rock is.
Epicentre means above the centre of the shaking.
Plates make up the Earth's crust.
items.explanation: Magma is underground and lava is on the surface. The epicentre is the surface point above the start of an earthquake.

items.prompt: Tectonic plates can push ___ each other, pull ___ from each other, or slide past each other.
hints: Think about what happens at a plate boundary.
Pushing together is the opposite of pulling apart.
Plates collide when they move towards each other.
items.explanation: At plate boundaries, plates collide, pull away or slide past. These movements cause earthquakes and volcanoes.

items.prompt: Why do scientists use readings from several seismograph stations to find the epicentre of an earthquake?

options.text: One station is enough to find the exact place.
options.why: A single station can only tell how far away the earthquake was.

options.text: Each station shows how far away the earthquake was, and the distances together point to one place.
More stations make the earthquake weaker.
options.why: Stations only record. They do not change the earthquake.

options.text: Stations stop the earthquake from happening.
options.why: Stations only measure.

hints: One station gives only a distance, not a direction.
Imagine drawing a circle around each station.
Where would the circles meet?
items.explanation: One station gives only the distance. With several stations, the circles of possible places cross at the epicentre.

items.prompt: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is where two plates are slowly pulling apart under the ocean. What do scientists expect to happen there?

options.text: Old crust sinks and the ocean gets narrower.
options.why: That happens where plates push together.

options.text: New crust forms from rising magma and the Atlantic Ocean slowly gets wider.
The sea floor stays the same for ever.
options.why: The plates are moving, so it changes.

options.text: The two continents crash into each other.
options.why: The plates are moving apart there, not together.

hints: What fills the gap when plates move apart?
Magma rises from the mantle.
Magma cools to make new rock.
items.explanation: As the plates pull apart, magma rises to fill the gap and cools into new crust. The ocean slowly widens.

items.prompt: Which layer of the Earth do we live on?

options.text: The mantle
options.why: The mantle is deep below our feet.

options.text: The inner core
options.why: The inner core is at the centre of the Earth.

options.text: The outer core
options.why: The outer core is far beneath the crust.

options.text: The crust

hints: It is the layer at the very outside.
Roads, houses and the sea floor sit on it.
It is the thinnest layer.
items.explanation: We live on the crust, the thin rocky layer at the surface.

items.prompt: Melted rock found below the Earth's surface is called ___.
hints: When it erupts it gets a different name.
It is found in a magma chamber.
It is the rock in a volcano before it erupts.
items.explanation: Magma is molten rock under the ground. When it erupts onto the surface, it is called lava.

items.prompt: True or false: The Earth has layers: a crust, a mantle and a core.

options.text: True
False

hints: Name the outside layer.
Think of an egg.
Crust, mantle, core.
items.explanation: The crust is the thin outside layer, the mantle is thick and hot, and the core is in the centre.

items.prompt: True or false: The Earth's crust is the thickest layer.

options.text: True
False

hints: Is the crust like a thin skin?
Which layer is thick?
The mantle is thickest.
items.explanation: The crust is the thinnest layer. The mantle is the thickest.

items.prompt: True or false: Earthquakes happen when pieces of the Earth's crust called plates move.

options.text: True
False

hints: What moves?
Plates slip.
Moving plates cause it.
items.explanation: Plates sometimes get stuck then slip suddenly, which shakes the ground.

items.prompt: True or false: Volcanoes are found in random places across the world.

options.text: True
False

hints: Where do plates meet?
Indonesia has many.
Edges of plates.
items.explanation: Many volcanoes lie along the edges of tectonic plates, like the Ring of Fire around the Pacific Ocean.

items.prompt: The hottest, innermost layer of the Earth is the ___.
hints: It is at the centre.
It is below the mantle.
It has four letters.
items.explanation: The core is the innermost and hottest layer of the Earth.
